stimulus_db: Educator: Few problems faced in daily life can be solved most effectively, if at all, by applying knowledge from any single academic discipline in isolation. Thus, schools should not require students to take courses in individual academic disciplines but should instead require them to take interdisciplinary courses.
stem_db: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the educator's argument?

choices_db.A: Problems faced in daily life usually can be solved effectively using only common sense.
choices_db.B: Most teachers are able to teach courses in a single academic discipline more effectively than they can teach interdisciplinary courses.
choices_db.C: Students who take only courses in individual academic disciplines are rarely able to combine knowledge from those disciplines.
choices_db.D: Most students who are required to take courses that cover only single disciplines can effectively solve many problems faced in daily life.
choices_db.E: Most interdisciplinary courses are not designed specifically to teach students how to solve problems faced in daily life.

bank.stem:
Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the
 educator’s argument?

choices.A: Problems faced in daily life usually can be solved effectively using only common sense.
choices.B: Most teachers are able to teach courses in a single academic discipline more effectively than they can teach interdisciplinary courses.
choices.C: Students who take only courses in individual academic disciplines are rarely able to combine knowledge from those disciplines.
choices.D: Most students who are required to take courses that cover only single disciplines can effectively solve many problems faced in daily life.
choices.E: Most interdisciplinary courses are not designed specifically to teach students how to solve problems faced in daily life.

steps.label: Conclusion (Thus)
steps.body: Schools should not require students to take courses in individual academic disciplines but should instead require them to take interdisciplinary courses.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: Most problems in daily life can't be solved most effectively, if at all, by applying knowledge from any single academic discipline in isolation.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body: We could spell out the Linking assumption here, If most problems can't be solved most effectively by applying knowledge from any single academic discipline in isolation, then schools shouldn't require students to take classes in single academic disciplines. But it seems more likely that the correct answer will be Defender style, ruling out some objection. GIven that ... most problems in daily life can't be solved best by applying knowledge from any single discipline. How could we still argue that ... schools should require students to take courses in individual disciplines? We could maybe say that solving problems in daily life involves applying knowledge from multiple disciplines, but it's too chaotic and disorganized to learn in that interdisciplinary style in school. Maybe it's better to require courses in individual academic disciplines, and then in daily life when these students face problems, they can just combine things they learned from these separate disciplines.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: Look for an answer like, "it is not easy to combine things you've learned from individual disciplines in order to face problems in daily life", or an answer linking the premise to the conclusion, or any other answer that, if negated, would hurt the argument.

notes.body: If common sense alone can solve most daily-life problems, that does not help the educator, and it does not contradict the premise either. The premise is a comparison: knowledge from a single discipline is rarely the most effective tool. Common sense solving problems "effectively" says nothing about which kind of course prepares students better. The answer cuts the same way against single-discipline and interdisciplinary courses, so it gives no reason to prefer the educator's recommendation. It does not strengthen the argument.

If teachers are better at teaching single-discipline courses, this creates a practical reason to keep the current system. The educator argues that interdisciplinary courses would better prepare students for daily life, but this answer introduces a significant cost: teaching quality would decline under the proposed change. Better teaching in single-discipline courses means students may actually learn more effectively from the existing format, even if the format does not perfectly mirror daily-life problem structures. This answer gives a reason to prefer the status quo rather than to adopt the educator's recommendation, which pushes against the conclusion rather than supporting it.

The educator's argument has a critical gap: it assumes that because daily-life problems require multi-disciplinary knowledge, the way courses are structured determines whether students can apply that knowledge effectively. This answer bridges that gap directly. If students who take only single-discipline courses are rarely able to combine knowledge from different disciplines on their own, then the course format is the bottleneck — not the students' ability or motivation. This means switching to interdisciplinary courses is not merely a theoretical improvement; it addresses a real, demonstrated failure of the current system. Students are not naturally acquiring cross-disciplinary integration skills from separate courses, so the courses themselves need to build that capability. This provides exactly the bridge premise the argument was missing and makes the conclusion significantly more compelling.

If most students who take only single-discipline courses can effectively solve many problems faced in daily life, that undermines the need for interdisciplinary courses. The educator's argument depends on the idea that single-discipline instruction leaves students poorly equipped for daily-life problems, which call for more than one field. But this answer says those students already handle many of those problems. If students already have the problem-solving ability the educator wants to build, then restructuring the courses looks unnecessary. This answer chips away at the very problem the educator's proposal is designed to solve, which weakens rather than strengthens the conclusion.

If most interdisciplinary courses are not designed to teach students how to solve daily-life problems, this undermines the educator's recommendation. The educator's entire reasoning is that daily-life problems require multi-disciplinary approaches, so courses should be interdisciplinary. But if the available interdisciplinary courses do not actually target daily-life problem-solving, then switching to them would not achieve the educator's stated goal. This introduces a practical problem with the proposed solution: the courses that exist do not match the purpose for which they are being recommended. At best this answer is irrelevant to whether the switch should happen in principle; at worst it suggests the switch would be ineffective in practice.
